claims.text: The modeled material is a single-crystal FeNiCrCoCu coating on a single-crystal Cu matrix with an FCC coating lattice.
At 300 K, the coating has a high density of dislocations and stacking faults.
The intervention is nanoindentation to 30 Å at 10 m/s at 300, 600, 900, and 1200 K.
Above 900 K, magneto-volume coupling and thermal expansion sharply increase the stacking-fault energy of FeNiCrCoCu.
Increasing stacking-fault energy suppresses partial-dislocation, stacking-fault, and nanotwin formation.
Thermal activation above 900 K causes rapid dislocation climb and annihilation in the coating.
Annihilation produces dislocation starvation and removes a dislocation network that normally stabilizes plastic flow.
Dislocation starvation and suppressed stacking-fault formation cause a transition from dislocation-mediated plasticity to localized amorphous-like shear banding.
The amorphous-like region behaves as a disordered fluid and promotes adhesive wear, producing higher friction and lower hardness.
Hardness peaks at 600 K because the dislocation network is stable.
Hardness and wear resistance drop sharply above 900 K.
The friction coefficient spikes at 1200 K.
The 1200 K friction spike coincides with a sudden increase in HCP-classified atoms that indicates disorder or phase transformation.
The 1200 K friction spike coincides with a decrease in total dislocation line length caused by starvation or annihilation.
At 600 K, the coating has high dislocation density and stable plasticity with lower friction.
Temperature-sensitive stacking-fault energy associated with magnetic effects is characteristic of relevant FCC HEAs.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to BCC HEAs because screw-dislocation mobility is governed differently.
The cited evidence does not directly establish an amorphization threshold for FeNiCrCoCu and provides stacking-fault-energy results only for CoCrFeMnNi up to 1000 K.
If mechanical annealing is responsible for the friction spike, maintaining a high initial dislocation density should suppress the spike and restore hardness.

If the friction spike persists despite high dislocation density, or tracks HCP atom count independently of dislocation density, thermal disorder rather than mechanical annealing is the primary driver.

contradictions.description: The mechanism predicts suppression of stacking faults, while the outcome predicts a sudden increase in HCP-classified atoms. In an FCC lattice, HCP-classified atoms commonly identify stacking-fault or twin environments, so the direction and interpretation of the HCP signal are internally inconsistent unless a distinct HCP phase-transformation signature is defined.

The main hypothesis says the response occurs rather than by mechanical annealing, yet rapid dislocation annihilation and starvation are central causal steps in its mechanism; the falsification rule then treats dislocation starvation as the mechanical-annealing alternative.
